results.title: Reproducible and reusable research: are journal data sharing policies meeting the mark? - PMC
results.content: The online author’s instructions and editorial policies for 318 biomedical journals were manually reviewed to analyze the journal’s data sharing requirements and characteristics. Moreover, while 65.7% of the journals in our study that required data sharing addressed the concept of reproducibility, as with earlier investigations, we found that most data sharing policies did not provide specific guidance on the practices that ensure data is maximally available and reusable. As an outcome, they produced the “Principles and Guidelines for Reporting Preclinical Research,” which included the recommendation that journals require that all of the data supporting a paper’s conclusion be made available as part of the review process and upon publication, that datasets be deposited to public repositories, and that datasets be bi-directionally linked to published articles in a way that ensures attribution (NIH, 2016b). Additionally, we examined the policies to determine the recommended data sharing method (e.g., a public repository or journal hosted), if data copyright or licensing recommendations were mentioned, the inclusion of instructions on how long the data should be made available, and if the policy noted reproducibility or analogous concepts. While only 21% of the journals in the study required data sharing (DSM 1 and 2), these journals published 42.1% of the citable items in 2013 and 2014 (23.6% and 24.9% of the citable items in 2013, 2014 after removing PLOS ONE) (Table 5). That is, a citable item that is open access is much more likely to be published in a journal with a data sharing requirement (DSM 1 or 2). However, even with PLOS ONE removed from the analysis, an open access article is still more likely to have been published in a journal with a data sharing requirement and the proportion of open access journals versus subscription journals that require data sharing is 16.0% vs 11.3% (Chi-square Test, *df* = 1, *p* < 2*e* − 16). While 65.7% of the journals in our study that required data sharing addressed the concept of reproducibility, as with earlier investigations (Piwowar, Chapman & Wendy, 2008; Sturges et al., 2015) we found that most data sharing policies did not provide specific guidance on the practices that ensure data is maximally available and reusable (DataONE, 2016; Starr et al., 2015). A review of journal policies for sharing research data.

results.title: Understanding the Role of a Cadastral Survey in Modern Land Management
results.content: # Understanding the Role of a Cadastral Survey in Modern Land Management. Whether you’re a land developer, government planner, or property investor, understanding cadastral surveying is key to avoiding costly mistakes and ensuring smooth land transactions. ## **What Is a Cadastral Survey?**. A cadastral survey is the backbone of legal land ownership. ## **Why Cadastral Surveys Matter More Than Ever**. In cities rapidly expanding and rural land being reclassified for development, cadastral surveys are more critical than ever. ## **Modern Uses of Cadastral Surveys**. Cadastral surveys aren’t just for buying land. For example, when working near a hydrographic survey vessel operation on coastal land, cadastral data must be aligned with maritime boundaries. Modern cadastral surveys power smart cities, support land restitution, and even help guide process plant operator decisions by defining legal land boundaries for industrial facilities. ## **Cadastral Surveys in the Digital Age**. Cadastral surveys may work quietly in the background, but they underpin every legal, financial, and planning decision involving land.

results.title: BLM National PLSS Public Land Survey System Polygons
results.content: BLM National PLSS Public Land Survey System Polygons | BLM GBP Hub. This member's profile information is private. BLM National PLSS Public Land Survey System Polygons. The CADNSDI or the Cadastral Publication Data Standard is the cadastral data component of the NSDI (National Spatial Data Infrastructure). This is the publication guideline for cadastral data that is intended to provide a common format and structure and content for cadastral information that can be made available across jurisdictional boundaries, providing a consistent and uniform cadastral data to meet business need that includes connections to the source information from the data stewards. The cadastral publication data is data provided by cadastral data producers in a standard form on a regular basis. Cadastral publication data has two primary components, land parcel data and cadastral reference data. It is important to recognize that the publication data are not the same as the operation and maintenance or production data. The production data is structured to optimize maintenance processes, is integrated with internal agency operations and contains much more detail than the publication data. The publication data is a subset of the more complete production data and is reformatted to meet a national standard so data can be integrated across jurisdictional boundaries and be presented in a consistent and standard form nationally. The primary source for the data is cadastral survey records housed by the BLM supplemented with local records and geographic control coordinates from states, counties as well as other federal agencies such as the USGS and USFS. The data has been converted from source documents to digital form and transferred into a GIS format that is compliant with FGDC Cadastral Data Content Standards and Guidelines for publication. This data is optimized for data publication and sharing rather than for specific 'production' or operation and maintenance. Please note that the data on this site, although published at regular intervals, may not be the most current PLSS data that is available from the BLM. Updates to the PLSS data at the BLM State Offices may have occurred since this data was published. To ensure users have the most current data, please contact the BLM PLSS Data Set Manager.
